  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Elisabetta Rocchetti
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Alfio Ferrara
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Literary Studies, Philology and Linguistics, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy<span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{elisabetta.rocchetti, alfio.ferrara}@unimi.it</span><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Correspondence:</span><a href="mailto:elisabetta.rocchetti@unimi.it" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">elisabetta.rocchetti@unimi.it</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> has shown that refusal in safety fine-tuned chat models is mediated by a single linear direction in the residual stream, recoverable by a difference-in-means (DiM) of harmful and harmless activations. We compare DiM-based interventions (activation addition and directional ablation) with two interventions derived from Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP)—nullspace projection and counterfactual flipping—on five open-weight chat models, asking whether INLP can match DiM at steering refusal and whether its richer parameterisation yields more tweakable interventions. INLP counterfactual flipping is competitive with DiM directional ablation on refusal suppression, while nullspace projection is weaker on most models. Applying each method at the layer selected by the other shows that flipping’s competitiveness is robust to this change while directional ablation’s is not, suggesting that DiM’s apparent edge is partly a property of its own selection procedure. Restricting INLP to the leading directions of the extracted subspace preserves most of the suppression effect at near-baseline perplexity, giving a tunable capability. Geometrically, the two INLP interventions land in qualitatively different regions of activation space: nullspace projection collapses transformed activations <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">between</em> the harmful and harmless clusters, while counterfactual flipping moves them into the opposite cluster, suggesting that the model encodes the absence of a concept differently from its opposite---an intriguing distinction that warrants further investigation in future work<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        Code available at: <a href="https://anonymous.4open.science/r/refusal_direction-5652/README.md" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://anonymous.4open.science/r/refusal_direction-5652/README.md</a></span></span></span>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Safety fine-tuned chat models tend to refuse harmful instructions while complying with harmless ones. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> have shown that this behaviour is mediated by a single linear direction in the residual stream, recoverable by averaging the difference between activations on harmful and harmless prompts. Adding this direction to the residual stream elicits refusal on harmless prompts; projecting it out suppresses refusal on harmful ones. The difference-in-means (DiM) construction is striking for its simplicity, and recent evaluations confirm that DiM is competitive with or stronger than more sophisticated extraction methods on alignment-related tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Im and Li, 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A natural question is whether other supervised primitives can recover something <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">different</em> that DiM cannot. We focus on Iterative Nullspace Projection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ravfogel et al., 2020</a>, INLP;)</cite>, a concept-erasure method that operates on a <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">subspace</em> of tunable dimensionality <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> rather than a single direction, and that supports a continuum of interventions through a parameterised projection <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> erases the concept (nullspace projection), while <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> reflects activations across the nullspace, producing a counterfactual representation that flips the concept while preserving orthogonal information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao and Linzen, 2023</a>)</cite>. To our knowledge, INLP-based interventions have not been systematically benchmarked alongside DiM—in particular, the AxBench evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> considers DiffMean, PCA, LAT, a probe and a supervised steering vector but not INLP.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We set out to compare DiM-based and INLP-based interventions on the refusal task, with two starting hypotheses about how INLP might fare:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H1 (effectiveness).</span> INLP-based interventions can match DiM at steering refusal. Both methods rest on the linear-representation hypothesis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and both estimate refusal-relevant directions from labelled contrastive activations, so we expect comparable behaviour despite their different geometric constructions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H2 (tweakability).</span> INLP’s richer parameterisation—a subspace of tunable dimensionality <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> together with a continuous family of operators <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>—can support intervention behaviours that single-direction DiM does not, in particular a tunable capability–effect trade-off via <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and qualitatively distinct operations via <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To probe these hypotheses we evaluate four interventions—DiM directional ablation, DiM activation addition, INLP nullspace projection (<math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>), and INLP counterfactual flipping (<math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>)—on five open-weight, safety fine-tuned chat models. We measure each intervention along an effectiveness axis (refusal suppression on harmful prompts and refusal injection on harmless ones) and a performance axis (perplexity, MMLU, and ARC). To understand <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> each intervention reshapes the residual stream we additionally inspect activation geometry in PCA space and run a structured completion analysis with an LLM judge. The work is preliminary; we discuss open questions and limitations in the Limitations section.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Supervised methods for extracting steering vectors.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Under the linear representation hypothesis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, concepts are encoded as directions in activation space, and these directions can be used to steer the model’s behaviour. A range of supervised techniques recover such vectors. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramani et al. (2022)</a></cite> optimise per-sentence latent vectors against a frozen decoder. Activation Addition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Contrastive Activation Addition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rimsky et al., 2024</a>)</cite> use single contrastive pairs and averaged contrastive differences, respectively—the latter being the same Mean-of-Differences estimator used by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> to isolate a refusal direction. Linear Artificial Tomography <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> extracts the top principal component of contrastive activations. Inference-Time Intervention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite> uses a probe weight on selected attention heads.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Concept erasure methods.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A separate but closely related family of techniques targets the inverse problem of <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">erasing</em> a concept rather than amplifying it. INLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ravfogel et al., 2020</a>)</cite> repeatedly trains linear classifiers and projects onto their nullspace, recovering a sequence of mutually orthogonal classifier directions that span a concept subspace. LEACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belrose et al., 2023</a>)</cite> provides a closed-form, minimally invasive linear erasure that defeats all linear classifiers. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao and Linzen (2023)</a></cite> use the INLP-derived subspace to <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">flip</em> a concept by reflecting activations across it, reversing BERT’s verb conjugation by intervening on the subject-number subspace. INLP is qualitatively distinct from the single-direction methods above in two ways relevant here: it operates on a subspace of tunable dimensionality <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, and the same extracted basis supports a continuum of interventions ranging from concept removal to counterfactual flipping—meaningful when the negative class corresponds to a genuine opposite (e.g., harmless vs. harmful) rather than to the absence of the concept.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Simple methods are often the strongest baselines.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2025)</a></cite> report that DiM clearly outperforms LAT, PCA, and sparse autoencoders on concept detection, while on steering all steering-vector approaches lag prompting and finetuning baselines. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Im and Li (2026)</a></cite> unify CAA, RepE, and ITI under a contrastive-pair objective, prove that the mean of differences is the optimal steering vector, and confirm that PCA and classifier variants tend to recover directions of incorrect orientation or magnitude. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belrose (2023)</a></cite> provide a complementary worst-case argument that interventions along the DiM direction are worst-case optimal in a related sense. None of these works benchmarks INLP-based interventions against DiM for steering, which is the gap we begin to fill.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Notation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a decoder-only transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020</a>)</cite> with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> blocks and residual-stream dimension <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. We write <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> for the residual-stream activation at the input of layer <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> at token position <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. We write <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> for the greedy completion produced on input <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. For chat models we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> and restrict our analysis to the post-instruction template tokens; we denote their positional indices by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both DiM and INLP are contrastive: given <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}^{+}\cup\mathcal{D}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>∪</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}^{+}\cup\mathcal{D}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> contains positive-class instructions and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> contains contrasting ones,</p>

<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We drop the layer index when no ambiguity arises.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Difference-in-means</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The DiM steering vector at layer <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> is the difference of class-mean activations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>)</cite>:</p>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with unit-norm counterpart <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{(l)}_{\text{DiM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>DiM</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{(l)}_{\text{DiM}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we use <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}^{(l)}_{\text{DiM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>DiM</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}^{(l)}_{\text{DiM}}</annotation></semantics></math> in two complementary interventions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">

<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Iterative Nullspace Projection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">INLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ravfogel et al., 2020</a>)</cite> retrieves a rowspace projector <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and its orthogonal complement <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}=\mathbb{I}-\mathbf{P}_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}=\mathbb{I}-\mathbf{P}_{R}</annotation></semantics></math>. At iteration <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> a linear classifier <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> is trained on the current activations to predict the class label; its unit-norm weight <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> defines a rank-one projector <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{R}^{(i)}=\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{R}^{(i)}=\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>. Activations are then projected onto the nullspace of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and the next classifier is trained. The procedure stops when no linear classifier achieves above-chance accuracy on a held-out set, yielding <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> orthogonal directions <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{1},\dots,\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{1},\dots,\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{R}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{P}_{N}=\mathbb{I}-\mathbf{P}_{R}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{R}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{P}_{N}=\mathbb{I}-\mathbf{P}_{R}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Restricting the sum to the first <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\leq n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\leq n</annotation></semantics></math> classifiers yields a partial rowspace projector <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{R}^{(\leq k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{R}^{(\leq k)}</annotation></semantics></math> and a corresponding partial nullspace projector <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}^{(\leq k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}^{(\leq k)}</annotation></semantics></math>, providing a way to control the size of the erased subspace. We construct the following interventions leveraging <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}^{(\leq k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}^{(\leq k)}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Nullspace projection (erasing, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>).</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Apply <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> directly:</p>

<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Counterfactual flipping (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>).</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao and Linzen (2023)</a></cite>, define</p>

<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and apply <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{h}^{(l)\prime}\leftarrow\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}\mathbf{h}^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐡</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo lspace="0em">′</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi>𝐏</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>α</mi></msub><mi>𝐡</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}^{(l)\prime}\leftarrow\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}\mathbf{h}^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>. <section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Refusal as case study</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate the generic contrastive sets as <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{+}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harmful</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{+}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{-}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmless}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harmless</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{-}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmless}}</annotation></semantics></math>, mirroring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>. From here on, <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the corresponding contrastive activations. We focus on refusal because it allows direct comparison with prior work on the same primitive and the same datasets; extending the comparison to other concepts is left to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Selecting layer and token position</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The vectors <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\text{DiM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>DiM</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\text{DiM}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> depend on a choice of <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math>. We follow the selection strategy of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>: candidates are ranked by a composite score that rewards suppression on harmful prompts, induction on harmless prompts, and penalises shifts in the final-logits distribution measured by KL with respect to the unintervened model. For INLP we additionally require that the first INLP classifier reaches a minimum validation accuracy. We depart from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> in applying each candidate intervention only at the layer from which it was extracted, rather than at every layer; this keeps the score fair across methods, since INLP-based interventions, especially full <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, have a stronger effect on logits than DiM. Empirically, the rankings are not significantly affected.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For INLP we run selection separately at four levels of <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math> (full <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>); <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=k_{0.9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.9</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=k_{0.9}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math>, the largest <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> such that the <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th classifier still reaches <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80\%</annotation></semantics></math> validation accuracy respectively. The main paper reports <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math>. Comparison of selected <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs across methods, and the rank correlations between selection scores, are reported in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Selection scores ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Evaluation metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate each intervention along an <em id="S3.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">effectiveness</em> axis (refusal-related behaviour) and a <em id="S3.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">performance</em> axis (general capabilities). All metrics are reported as a signed difference <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=m_{\text{int}}-m_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mtext>int</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=m_{\text{int}}-m_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math> from the unintervened baseline, oriented so that higher always means more desirable.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effectiveness.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the harmful test set <math id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{\text{(test)}}_{\text{harmful}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>harmful</mtext><mtext>(test)</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{\text{(test)}}_{\text{harmful}}</annotation></semantics></math> we compute three components: (i) <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-refusal harmful</span>, the substring-matching non-refusal rate of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>; (ii) <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unsafe harmful</span>, the LlamaGuard 2 unsafety rate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; and (iii) <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-refusal harmful (judge)</span>, an LLM-judge non-refusal rate using a Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct judge constrained to a structured JSON schema (Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Judge protocol ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>). On the harmless test set we compute the corresponding <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refusal harmless</span> and <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refusal harmless (judge)</span> rates. All completions are produced with greedy decoding at 256 new tokens. Throughout, we report the substring-based components as the headline effectiveness metrics and reserve the judge-based ones as diagnostics; Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> discusses why, including a calibrated audit of the substring/judge disagreement.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Performance.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report perplexity on held-out text from <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Alpaca</span> and <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Pile</span> as a relative change clipped to <math id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>, and 5-shot accuracy on <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ARC</span>-Challenge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2018</a>)</cite> as absolute changes.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental setup</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s construction. The harmful train set (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\text{train}}=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\text{train}}=128</annotation></semantics></math>) samples <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AdvBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MaliciousInstruct</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TDC2023</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; the harmful val set (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\text{val}}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\text{val}}=32</annotation></semantics></math>) draws from <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HarmBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The harmless train and val sets (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>) draw from <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Alpaca</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. For evaluation we use the full <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\text{test}}=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\text{test}}=100</annotation></semantics></math> harmful instructions from <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">JailbreakBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> (covering ten harm categories) and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> harmless instructions from a fixed-seed split of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Alpaca</span> disjoint from train/val. Capability evaluations use a held-out subset of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Pile</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Alpaca</span> for perplexity, a <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500</annotation></semantics></math>-question stratified sample of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> for 5-shot knowledge, and the 4-choice subset of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ARC</span>-Challenge with 5-shot prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on five open-weight, safety fine-tuned chat models drawn from five families: <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Gemma</span> 2B-IT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Qwen</span> 1.8B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Yi</span> 6B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">AI et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Llama-2</span> 7B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Llama-3</span> 8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. As this is a preliminary work, we restrict to the smallest model in each family. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> report that the qualitative behaviour of the DiM refusal direction is largely preserved at scale on the same families; whether this holds for INLP-based interventions is left to future work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Per-model summary at the selected <math id="S4.T1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math>. All values are <math id="S4.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> from baseline, oriented so that higher is better; <math id="S4.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> denotes SE for effectiveness columns and SD for performance columns. PPL deltas use median per-example perplexity; SDs above <math id="S4.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> are shown as <math id="S4.T1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gg\!1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≫</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gg\!1000</annotation></semantics></math>. Performance columns average two benchmarks each; their SDs are combined as <math id="S4.T1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}}/n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></msqrt><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}}/n</annotation></semantics></math>. Interventions are applied only to the selected component.</figcaption>
