<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present results in three steps: aggregate effectiveness and performance (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Effectiveness and performance ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>); a geometric view of how each intervention reshapes the residual stream (§<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>); and a structured completion analysis surfacing qualitative differences (§<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Completion analysis ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>).
All main-paper results report interventions applied only to the selected <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> component, so that DiM and INLP are compared on equal footing; the variant where interventions are applied at every layer is reported in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E All results tables ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Effectiveness and performance</h3>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Counterfactual flipping matches directional ablation on refusal suppression.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across all five models, counterfactual flipping reaches non-refusal scores comparable to, and in several cases exceeding, those of directional ablation; the same pattern holds on the LlamaGuard 2 unsafety metric. Nullspace projection is consistently weaker: it suppresses refusal effectively only on Gemma, Yi, and to some extent Llama-3, partially fails on Qwen, and fails on Llama-2. This asymmetry suggests that different models organise the refusal subspace differently. One possibility is that harmful and harmless representations are simply farther apart in some models than others; another is that models maintain a dedicated subspace for representing the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">absence</span> of information about harmfulness, distinct from both the harmfulness subspace and its opposite.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ActAdd dominates harmless-prompt refusal injection but pays a coherence cost.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On harmless prompts, ActAdd reaches <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> Refusal harmless <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq+0.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.86</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq+0.86</annotation></semantics></math> on every model and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1.00</annotation></semantics></math> on Llama-3, while no counterfactual-flip variant exceeds <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.4</annotation></semantics></math>. The advantage is partly a measurement artefact: the median-PPL column shows that ActAdd is the worst intervention in language-modelling loss, and Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Completion analysis ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> confirms that many ActAdd completions are degenerate, repeating short refusal templates. Counterfactual flipping produces a smaller but qualitatively cleaner injection effect.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Erasing fewer directions improves capability preservation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On Gemma, Yi, Llama-2, and Llama-3, restricting INLP to <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> leaves harmful-prompt non-refusal essentially unchanged while reducing perplexity degradation. Qwen is the exception: <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math> <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decreases</em> non-refusal and incurs the largest perplexity hit in the table (<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.71</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.71</annotation></semantics></math>), while <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> recovers a clean <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.62" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.62</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.62</annotation></semantics></math> non-refusal score with negligible perplexity change. The directions retained by INLP beyond the strong-classifier threshold appear to encode information correlated with refusal but not causally responsible for it on this model. More broadly, <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> keeps all five models within <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math> of baseline perplexity, and we adopt it as the operating point for the analyses below. The MMLU+ARC column shows no meaningful drop in 5-shot accuracy under any intervention.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Selection picks different layers and token positions.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The DiM and INLP selection scores do not converge on the same <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math>. Across all models, the layer chosen by DiM differs from the one chosen by INLP by at least one layer, and the chosen post-instruction token position often differs too. Despite this, the rankings induced by the two scores are broadly similar, especially at <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math>; Spearman correlations and top-3 agreement are reported in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Selection scores ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. For time and compute reasons the selection scores for both INLP-based interventions are computed using nullspace projection only. Given the more promising results of counterfactual flipping, we expect a flipping-based selection to produce an even better operating point.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-site application reveals flipping’s robustness and narrows DiM’s edge.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since DiM and INLP select different <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> pairs, the method-level gaps in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> could be genuine properties of each intervention or artefacts of comparing each method at its own hand-picked layer. We disentangle the two by applying each method also at the <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> selected by the <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">other</em>, holding everything else fixed. The full grid is reported in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Cross-site comparison: same-site vs. cross-site ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> (Table <a href="#A2.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix B Cross-site comparison: same-site vs. cross-site ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>); Figure <a href="#S5.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Cross-site application reveals flipping’s robustness and narrows DiM’s edge. ‣ 5.1 Effectiveness and performance ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarises the headline pattern.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.13720v2/cross_method_dumbbell.svg" id="S5.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/538;" width="476" height="538"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Same-site vs. cross-site effectiveness and perplexity, one panel per model. For each intervention, three dumbbells connect the same-site value (open circle, the operating point used in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) to the cross-site value (filled triangle: cross-site improved; inverted triangle: cross-site worsened), for non-refusal on harmful prompts (blue), refusal injection on harmless prompts (green), and median perplexity on Pile+Alpaca (red). Directional ablation is applied at INLP’s selected layer and vice versa. Values are <math id="S5.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> from baseline, oriented so that higher is better.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Counterfactual flipping at <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math> is the most layer-robust intervention in the grid: it holds steady or improves at the cross-site layer on all five models, and its harmless-side injection numbers rise substantially in four of five cases. Most notably, Qwen’s counterfactual-flip cell in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>—the one case where the intervention <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reduced</em> non-refusal (<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.13</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.13</annotation></semantics></math>)—reaches <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.70</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.70</annotation></semantics></math> at DiM’s layer, indicating that this negative result is a selection-score artefact rather than a genuine weakness of the intervention.
The exception is <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> on Llama-3, where flipping falls from <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.96</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.96</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.12</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.12</annotation></semantics></math>.
Directional ablation shows the opposite pattern: it collapses at INLP’s selected layer on three of five models (Qwen <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="+0.67\!\to\!+0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.608em;" width="0.608em"><mo>+</mo></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.484em;" width="0.484em"><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mpadded><mo>+</mo><mn>0.03</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.67\!\to\!+0.03</annotation></semantics></math>; Llama-2 <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="+0.46\!\to\!+0.06" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.608em;" width="0.608em"><mo>+</mo></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.484em;" width="0.484em"><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mpadded><mo>+</mo><mn>0.06</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.46\!\to\!+0.06</annotation></semantics></math>; Llama-3 <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="+0.95\!\to\!+0.20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.608em;" width="0.608em"><mo>+</mo></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.484em;" width="0.484em"><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mpadded><mo>+</mo><mn>0.20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.95\!\to\!+0.20</annotation></semantics></math>), suggesting that DiM’s apparent simplicity and robustness in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is itself partly a function of its own selection procedure rather than an intrinsic property of the intervention.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summary.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H1</span> (effectiveness) is partially borne out: INLP counterfactual flipping is on par with DiM directional ablation at suppressing refusal, but nullspace projection is consistently weaker, and on harmless-side refusal injection ActAdd remains the strongest intervention by surface metrics—with a degeneracy-related caveat we revisit in Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Completion analysis ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.
The cross-site check above sharpens this reading: counterfactual flipping’s competitiveness with directional ablation survives a change of layer, while directional ablation’s own strength is comparatively layer-dependent, so the aggregate comparison in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> may understate INLP’s robustness relative to DiM.
<span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H2</span> (tweakability) is supported by the <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-based capability–effect trade-off above and, more interestingly, by the fact that the same extracted subspace yields two qualitatively distinct interventions through the choice of <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, a possibility DiM does not afford. The qualitative difference between <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> is most visible in activation geometry, which we examine next.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Geometric view: absence vs. opposite</h3>

<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.13720v2/paper_pca_all_models_acc80.png" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/474;" width="476" height="474" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Two-dimensional PCA visualisation of intervention effects in residual-stream space, computed at the input of the selected transformer block at the selected post-instruction token position. The first axis is fixed to the harmful–harmless centroid direction, so horizontal movement corresponds to movement along the refusal axis. <span id="S5.F2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Red/blue dots:</span> original harmful/harmless activations, with dark stars marking class centroids. <span id="S5.F2.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Orange crosses:</span> transformed harmful activations under a refusal-removal intervention. <span id="S5.F2.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Green pluses:</span> transformed harmless activations under a refusal-injection intervention. Rows are models; columns are interventions. Each (model, intervention family) cell uses its own coordinate system, so absolute distances are not comparable across cells; the relative positioning within each cell is the object of interest. <em id="S5.F2.13" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Directional ablation</em> collapses both classes onto the harmless side; <em id="S5.F2.14" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ActAdd</em> and <em id="S5.F2.15" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">counterfactual flipping</em> produce a two-way swap; <em id="S5.F2.16" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">nullspace projection</em> collapses both classes into a region <em id="S5.F2.17" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">between</em> the two clusters.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> visualises the effect of each intervention by projecting activations into a 2D PCA space whose first axis is fixed to the harmful–harmless centroid direction; horizontal movement corresponds to movement along the refusal axis. The four interventions trace four qualitatively distinct patterns, consistent across all five models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Directional ablation</em> collapses both classes onto the harmless side of the refusal axis, consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s framing of ablation as one-sided—it removes the refusal direction without producing its opposite. <em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ActAdd</em> produces a cleaner two-way swap: transformed harmful-to-harmless and harmless-to-harmful points end up close to the centroids of their respective target classes. <em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Counterfactual flipping</em> (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>) likewise produces a two-way swap. <em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Nullspace projection</em> (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>) produces the most striking pattern: transformed points collapse into a region <em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">between</em> the harmful and harmless clusters, rather than into either of them.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Absence-of-concept differs from concept-opposite.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The nullspace pattern is informative: it suggests, tentatively, that the model encodes the absence of refusal information differently from the opposite of refusal. Erasing the refusal subspace (nullspace projection) leaves the activation in an under-determined region of representation space; reflecting across that subspace (counterfactual flipping) produces an activation that resembles the opposite class. In this view, directional ablation behaves more like a one-sided counterfactual flip than a true ablation, since it actively pushes harmful activations onto the harmless side rather than to a neutral region. A quantitative target-group-fit measure confirms this visual impression: counterfactual flipping lands closest to the opposite-class centroid in both directions across most models, while nullspace projection sits noticeably farther away, consistent with the absence-region reading (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional PCA results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Target-group fit in 2D PCA ‣ Appendix C Additional PCA results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). The same qualitative behaviour appears in all five models, though we emphasise that this remains preliminary: refusal is a case where “absence of harmfulness” and “opposite of harmfulness” are not cleanly separated semantically, and disentangling the two requires concepts where the negative class is genuinely either an opposite or a neutral state. We return to this point in the Limitations section as the main direction the present results call for.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Completion analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A finer-grained view of what lies beneath the aggregate refusal rates is shown in Figures <a href="#A4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Per-model summary of judge-side outcomes. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> and <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Refusal-reason categories. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, both deferred to Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.
Figure <a href="#A4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Per-model summary of judge-side outcomes. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> reports four judge-side outcome variables: <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">initial refusal then compliance</em> (the model opens with a canonical refusal phrase but ultimately satisfies the request), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">partial request satisfaction</em> (on-task but incomplete, generic, or hedged output, as opposed to a full refusal or a fully compliant response), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">looping or repetitive output</em> (flagged when the completion repeats the same content two or more times at the literal, near-literal, or token level), and <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">asks for more context</em> (flagged when the completion explicitly requests clarification before proceeding). Figure <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Refusal-reason categories. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> reports the refusal-reason composition among completions the judge labels as refusals: <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unethical or illegal</em> (the model explicitly frames the task as harmful, illegal, or against policy), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusing opposite task</em> (the model substitutes a different or opposite task in place of the requested one), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lacks ability</em> (the model cites a capability or knowledge limitation), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">illogical reason</em> (the cited reason does not coherently support refusal), <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no reason given</em> (refusal with no stated justification), and <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.10" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">legit other</em> (a sensible reason not fitting any of the above). We comment patterns that are most relevant for the DiM/INLP comparison.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ActAdd’s harmless-side advantage is partly degeneracy.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The most striking pattern in Figure <a href="#A4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Per-model summary of judge-side outcomes. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> is the prevalence of looping completions under ActAdd, consistent with the perplexity spikes in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. On harmless prompts many of these degenerate outputs happen to contain a refusal phrase, which means the high <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> Refusal harmless under ActAdd is partly a measurement artefact of repetitive generation. A milder version of the same pattern appears for Qwen under counterfactual flipping with <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math>, corroborating the perplexity hit on that cell (and motivating the use of <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">INLP refusals are more often principled, but coverage is uneven.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Refusal-reason categories. ‣ D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows that on harmful prompts the four interventions are qualitatively indistinguishable from baseline: surviving refusals are dominated by ethics-framing (<em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unethical or illegal</em>, <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 77\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>77</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 77\%</annotation></semantics></math> on every cell) with an opposite-task tail consistent with each model’s baseline tendency. Interventions differ in <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how much</em> they suppress refusal but not in <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what kind</em> survives. On harmless prompts the picture is different: ActAdd-induced refusals are ethics-framed in surface terms but co-occur with substantial shares of non-principled tags whose profile varies by model (e.g., <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lacks ability</em> on Gemma, <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no reason given</em> on Yi/Llama-3, <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">illogical reason</em> on Qwen, <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusing opposite task</em> on Llama-2). The high <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no reason given</em> shares line up with the looping behaviour above. Counterfactual flipping at <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> injects refusal less often than ActAdd—as Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> establishes—but on the cells with non-trivial denominators (Qwen, Llama-3) the induced refusals are more often principled. Four further pooled views (judge-label composition, request satisfaction, harm-category heatmap, coherence side-effects) are reported alongside these breakdowns in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 What the LLM judge sees: behavioural decomposition ‣ Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">INLP produces more clarification-seeking responses on harmless prompts.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A smaller but consistent pattern: INLP variants surface refusal-like phrasings (<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“I’m not sure I understand…”</span>) followed by compliance, which substring matching counts as refusals while the LLM judge does not. This means the harmless-side refusal rate for counterfactual flipping in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is likely inflated relative to DiM when measured by substring matching alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Substring vs. judge measurement</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The choice of refusal metric matters for the comparison. Substring matching and the LLM judge agree on <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="84\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>84</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">84\%</annotation></semantics></math> of completions across our experimental grid; the disagreement is concentrated on harmful prompts (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>25.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.6\%</annotation></semantics></math>) and grows monotonically with intervention aggressiveness, from <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> at baseline to <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 42\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>42</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 42\%</annotation></semantics></math> under counterfactual flipping with <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>—i.e., the regime where measurement reliability matters most. A stratified hand-coded audit indicates that both protocols are biased on harmful prompts but the judge’s bias is larger: it systematically over-fires on taboo-topic prompts whose response contains the requested harmful content wrapped in a moralising disclaimer. We adopt substring matching as the primary headline metric on the grounds that the substring rate is closer to the audited true rate than the raw judge rate, and that the residual correction is approximately uniform across models and methods so that the <em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">relative</em> ordering of methods is preserved. However, we hypothesise that by using a larger judge model, we can achieve better and less biased results. The full audit is reported in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented a preliminary comparison of DiM-based and INLP-based linear interventions for refusal in safety fine-tuned chat models, organised around two starting hypotheses. <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H1</span> (effectiveness) is partially supported: INLP counterfactual flipping is competitive with DiM directional ablation at refusal suppression—and a cross-site check, applying each method at the other’s selected layer, shows that this competitiveness survives a change of operating point while directional ablation’s own strength does not—while INLP nullspace projection is consistently weaker, and ActAdd remains the strongest intervention for harmless-side refusal injection by surface metrics (with a degeneracy caveat, (with a degeneracy caveat, §<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Completion analysis ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>). <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H2</span> (tweakability) is supported by INLP’s <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-based capability–effect trade-off and, more interestingly, by the fact that the same extracted subspace supports two qualitatively distinct interventions through <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>—a flexibility DiM does not afford. Beyond these expected outcomes, the comparison surfaced a geometric observation: nullspace projection and counterfactual flipping leave transformed activations in qualitatively different regions of the residual stream, providing tentative evidence that the model encodes the absence of refusal differently from its opposite. This reading is preliminary, and refusal is a poor case for sharpening it, for reasons we detail under <em id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Beyond refusal</em> in the Limitations section, which also outlines the case studies, selection-procedure refinements, and measurement improvements needed before stronger conclusions can be drawn. DiM remains the simpler primitive and the stronger baseline for refusal suppression at its own selected layer, but INLP’s richer primitive deserves further study.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Beyond refusal: case studies on concepts with semantic opposites.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The strongest signal in our results is the geometric difference between nullspace projection and counterfactual flipping in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, which we read tentatively as the model encoding the absence of a concept differently from its opposite. Refusal, however, is a poor case for sharpening this reading: the contrast set (harmful vs. harmless) blurs the absence/opposite distinction at the semantic level, since “harmless” is at once the negation of harmful and a class with its own positive content. Concepts with explicit semantic structure are needed to disentangle the two readings. Pronoun gender (“he”/“she” as semantic opposites and “it” as an approximate absence), truthfulness vs. falsehood, sentiment polarity, and simpler binary attributes with a clear neutral state are all natural test beds. Replicating the <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> comparison on such concepts—and inspecting the corresponding activation geometry—is the main direction this preliminary work calls for, and the one needed before the absence-vs.-opposite reading can be made rigorous.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Selection procedure for INLP.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The selection scores used to pick <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> are computed using nullspace projection only. The promising results of counterfactual flipping suggest that a flipping-based selection would identify a different operating point and likely improve the harmless-side injection numbers in particular. Running the full grid with separate selection scores for <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math> is the most direct extension.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison with LEACE.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LEACE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belrose et al., 2023</a>)</cite> provides a closed-form, minimally invasive linear erasure that provably defeats all linear classifiers while preserving as much structure in the representation as possible. Unlike INLP, which builds the erased subspace iteratively through a sequence of classifiers, LEACE computes the erasure in a single pass and is guaranteed to be the <em id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">least disruptive</em> projection consistent with defeating linear decoding. Benchmarking LEACE alongside INLP and DiM would clarify whether the geometric pattern we observe (absence vs. opposite) is robust across different concept-erasure primitives, and whether LEACE’s minimality constraint translates into a better capability–effectiveness trade-off than INLP’s <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-based tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Larger models.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We restrict our experiments to the smallest model in each of five families. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> report on <math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>13</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13</annotation></semantics></math>B–<math id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>72</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72</annotation></semantics></math>B variants of the same families and find the qualitative behaviour of the DiM refusal direction largely preserved at scale. Whether INLP-based interventions scale similarly, and whether the gap between the two methods narrows or widens, is open.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tighter measurement.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM-as-a-judge: protocol, behavioural decomposition, and comparison with substring matching ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> discusses several concrete improvements to refusal measurement (mitigating the judge’s taboo-topic over-fire with a response-only second pass, augmenting the substring keyword list with the non-canonical phrasings exposed by the audit, training a small opposite-task detector). Tightening the bracketing on the true refusal rate would in particular sharpen the harmless-side comparison between counterfactual flipping and ActAdd.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Other limitations.</h5>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The contrastive sets are constructed exactly as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which makes our results directly comparable but inherits any distributional biases of those datasets. We use a single LLM judge (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) and report a calibrated audit of its biases; running the same audit with a stronger judge model could change the absolute numbers in Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Substring vs. judge measurement ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>, though we expect the ordering of methods to be robust.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Selection scores</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix reports diagnostic information about the per-method selection procedure of Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Selecting layer and token position ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>. Table <a href="#A1.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix A Selection scores ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> lists the top three (post-instruction token position, layer) pairs by composite score for each (model, intervention) cell. Token positions are negative offsets from the end of the chat template (so position <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> is the final post-instruction token). Across models, INLP-based interventions tend to select earlier-layer activations than directional ablation, and the gap shrinks as <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> decreases.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A1.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Appendix A Selection scores ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the Spearman rank correlation between the selection scores assigned to each <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> pair under different methods. Across all five models, DiM and INLP at <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> produce highly correlated rankings (typically <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0.7</annotation></semantics></math>), supporting the claim that the two extraction methods capture related but not identical information about refusal even when their top-1 choices differ.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Top selection-score position/layer pairs by model and intervention. <section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Cross-site comparison: same-site vs. cross-site</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix reports the full grid underlying the cross-site robustness check summarised in Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Effectiveness and performance ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>. For each (model, method) cell, we report two rows: the <em id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">same-site</em> value, at the <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> selected for that method (reproducing Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), and the <em id="A2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-site</em> value, at the <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l,t)</annotation></semantics></math> selected for the <em id="A2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">other</em> extraction primitive—the INLP-selected layer for DiM interventions, and the DiM-selected layer for INLP interventions. INLP interventions are reported at both <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=n</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0.8</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{0.8}</annotation></semantics></math>, so that the interaction between subspace size and layer choice is visible. All other experimental settings (datasets, decoding, metrics) match Section <a href="#S3.SS6" title="3.6 Evaluation metrics ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Target-group fit in 2D PCA</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix reports in full the target-group-fit analysis summarised in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>: for each intervention, how well transformed activations fit the opposite-class cluster relative to native examples of that class. Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Target-group fit in 2D PCA ‣ Appendix C Additional PCA results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the violins in the same 2D PCA projection used in Figure <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Let <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the harmless and harmful activations at the selected layer and token position, with centroids <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> be the same 2D PCA projection used in Figure <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 5.2 Geometric view: absence vs. opposite ‣ 5 Results ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For an intervention <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> with refusal-injection transform <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="T_{\bullet}^{(+\to-)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mo>∙</mo></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">+</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\bullet}^{(+\to-)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the harmless-to-harmful target-fit ratio for <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}\in\mathbf{H}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐡</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}\in\mathbf{H}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>

<p id="A3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and the harmful-to-harmless ratio is symmetric. Counterfactual flipping (<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=2</annotation></semantics></math>) produces ratios closest to <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> in both directions across most models, indicating that flipped activations resemble native members of the target class. ActAdd shows substantially wider violins on the harmful-to-harmless side, with a long tail above <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, consistent with the perplexity degradation observed for ActAdd in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Models. ‣ 4 Experimental setup ‣ Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Nullspace projection sits noticeably farther from the target centroid than counterfactual flipping, again consistent with the absence-region interpretation.</p>
